title: The Guest and the Fast
premise: A fictional medieval Benedictine guesthouse asks how hospitality and fasting can coexist. This is one Latin-Christian rule and a particular case, not a universal religion or a proof of doctrine.

items.label: Basin
items.description: A basin ready for washing water.

items.label: Basket
items.description: A basket for carrying the guest’s meal.

items.label: Bread
items.description: A loaf ready to offer the traveller.

items.label: Brothers timetable
items.description: The brothers’ ordinary fasting schedule continues today. A guest at the superior’s table does not cancel it.

items.label: Calendar
items.description: In this fictional case, today is an ordinary fast—not one of the principal fasts excluded from the guest exception.

items.label: Chapter 53
items.description: Rule 53 distinguishes roles and days: the superior may break a fast for a guest, except on a principal fast that cannot be broken. Other brothers keep their usual practice.

items.label: Community fast note
items.description: The brothers keep the usual fast. The guest-related exception for their superior does not extend to the whole community.

items.label: Fasting rule
items.description: The brothers follow the community’s usual fasting practice. Does welcoming a guest change that for everyone?

items.label: Guest account
items.description: The traveller says: “I arrived hungry, and worried that my arrival would interrupt everyone’s day.” An invented voice, not a historical quotation.

items.label: Guest meal
items.description: The bread is gathered in its basket, ready for the guest.

items.label: Guest table
items.description: The traveller’s meal is on the laid table.

items.label: Guest washstand
items.description: Water and linen are ready for the traveller to wash.

items.label: Hospitality passage
items.description: In this Benedictine rule, guests are welcomed with care. The guest and superior have a separate kitchen; this is a particular community’s arrangement.

items.label: Hospitality question
items.description: Must feeding the guest mean that every brother breaks the fast—or does the rule distinguish their roles?

items.label: Host exception
items.description: A limited exception concerns the superior receiving the guest. It does not suspend the brothers’ fast, and does not apply to an unbreakable principal fast.

items.label: Host permission
items.description: Today’s stipulated ordinary fast permits the superior to eat with the guest. The permission is limited to this case.

items.label: Laid table
items.description: The guest dining table is laid with linen.

items.label: Linen
items.description: Clean linen for washing or laying the dining table.

items.label: Ordinary fast day
items.description: The calendar identifies today as an ordinary fast; the principal-fast exclusion does not apply to this fictional day.

items.label: Shared table
items.description: The superior’s place is prepared beside the guest’s. The brothers’ usual fasting practice continues elsewhere.

items.label: Table
items.description: The table in the adjoining guest dining room.

items.label: Washing basin
items.description: The basin has water, ready for the washstand.

items.label: Water
items.description: Water for the guest’s washstand.

items.label: Welcome reading
items.description: The guest should be cared for. That does not yet tell us who, besides the guest, may eat today.

In this fictional case the calendar identifies an ordinary fast, not an unbreakable principal fast.
Must receiving a guest mean abandoning the fast for the whole community? The question exposes a tension, not a contradiction proved by the game.
Chapter53 distinguishes the superior receiving a guest from the other brothers, and ordinary fasts from principal fasts. The exception is limited, not a repeal.
For this ordinary fast, the superior may eat with the guest. The other brothers keep their usual fasting practice.

stages.title: At the guesthouse gate
stages.speaker: The guestmaster
stages.motivation: A traveller has arrived tired and hungry. Prepare a washstand, and put a meal in the guesthouse.

area.label: At the guesthouse gate
area.travelText: We are taking the useful things with us. Earlier creations remain where we made them.

objectives.text: Put the guest meal in the Guesthouse.

stages.completionText: The guest has a meal waiting, and the washstand is ready. Now the novice brings a question about today’s fast.

stages.title: A guest on a fast day
stages.speaker: The novice
stages.motivation: Today is a fast. Can our superior eat with the traveller while the brothers keep it? Find the host’s permission, and make a note of the community’s fast.

area.label: A guest on a fast day
area.travelText: We are taking the useful things with us. Earlier creations remain where we made them.

caches.label: The guestmaster’s desk
caches.narrative: The desk holds the Rule, a fasting schedule, today’s calendar and the traveller’s account. We are considering an ordinary fast, not a principal fast.

objectives.text: Establish the host’s permission for this day.
Make the note preserving the community’s fast.

stages.completionText: For this ordinary fast, the host may eat with the guest; the brothers keep their usual practice. Both parts of the rule remain visible.

stages.title: Room at the table
stages.speaker: The guestmaster
stages.motivation: The rule makes room for our guest without asking the whole community to stop its practice. Prepare the shared table.

area.label: Room at the table
area.travelText: We are taking the useful things with us. Earlier creations remain where we made them.

caches.label: The guest dining room
caches.narrative: The adjoining room has a table. The meal and linen come with us.

stages.completionText: The shared table is prepared. Hospitality has made room for the traveller without turning one limited exception into a rule for everyone.

sources.title: Rule of Benedict, chapter53, especially verses10–11 and16
sources.note: Primary translation. Host exception, principal-fast limitation and other brothers’ continued practice distinguish this case.

notes: Explicitly a fictional Benedictine case grounded in one primary text, not all Christian practice or all religions.
An ordinary fast is a stipulated story fact; the recipe does not calculate a real liturgical calendar.
The rule makes distinct roles and conditions matter. Gameplay still risks document assembly; test before expanding.
The meal is carried from the former guesthouse area into its adjoining dining room, not conjured by the argument.
